nameStory: Grey alder gets its name from the distinctive grayish bark that becomes more prominent as the shrub matures. It's also called 'speckled alder' because the bark often shows light-colored spots or speckles, creating a mottled appearance that catches the eye along wetland edges.
description: Grey alder is a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree that typically grows 10-20 feet tall, though it can reach up to 30 feet in ideal conditions. It forms dense thickets along streams, pond edges, and wet areas through its ability to spread by underground runners. The plant has an upright, bushy growth habit with multiple stems arising from the base, and its oval leaves have serrated edges that give them a saw-toothed appearance.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish bark with light speckles or patches, especially noticeable on older stems. The bark feels relatively smooth to the touch and often has a slightly mottled appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with sharply serrated (saw-toothed) edges and prominent parallel veins. The leaves feel slightly rough and have a matte green surface that turns yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub forming dense colonies through underground runners. Individual stems are slender and often lean slightly, creating a thicket-like appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces both male and female catkins on the same plant in early spring. Male catkins are long, drooping, and yellowish, while female catkins are shorter and reddish-brown.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small woody cones about half an inch long that persist through winter. These cone-like fruits start green and turn brown, releasing tiny winged seeds when mature.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are reddish-brown and slightly sticky to the touch, arranged alternately along the twigs. The buds have a somewhat pointed oval shape.

habitat: Grey alder thrives in wet soils and is commonly found along stream banks, pond edges, swamps, and other wetland margins throughout New England. It tolerates flooding well and often forms the dominant shrub layer in these wet areas. You'll also find it in wet meadows and the edges of beaver ponds, often growing alongside willows and red maples.

seasonality.spring: Catkins appear in early spring before the leaves emerge, with drooping yellow male catkins being quite conspicuous. New leaves unfurl in late spring with a fresh green color.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage displays the characteristic serrated leaves and parallel venation pattern. Small cone-like fruits begin developing and are green at first.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, and the woody cones mature to brown. The speckled bark becomes more noticeable as foliage thins.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show off the distinctive grayish, speckled bark and persistent brown cones. Reddish-brown buds are visible along the twigs.

funFact: Grey alder is a natural soil improver that can actually make nitrogen fertilizer from thin air! Like other alders, it has special root nodules containing bacteria that capture nitrogen from the atmosphere and convert it into nutrients that enrich the soil for other plants.
confusionNotes: Grey alder is most often confused with smooth alder, but grey alder has distinctly speckled grayish bark while smooth alder has darker, smoother bark. Remember: 'Grey' alder = 'Grayish' bark with speckles, while 'smooth' alder = smoother, darker bark.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'tag alder' is an old regional name still heard in parts of New England, referring to the plant's tendency to 'tag along' streams and waterways. Despite being called an alder 'tree,' grey alder typically grows as a large shrub and rarely develops a single dominant trunk like true trees.
compareHints: Among New England alders, grey alder is distinguished by its speckled grayish bark and multi-stemmed shrubby growth habit. Green alder is typically smaller and found at higher elevations, while smooth alder has darker, less speckled bark. Common alder, less frequent in our region, tends to grow larger and has darker bark with more prominent horizontal markings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Green alder stands out from its New England relatives by its greenish young bark - gray alder has consistently gray bark, common alder tends to be larger and more tree-like, and smooth alder has smoother leaf undersides and prefers warmer areas.
Common alder differs from gray alder by having more rounded leaves with blunt tips versus gray alder's more pointed, oval leaves.
Compared to gray alder, smooth alder has much smoother bark and forms denser thickets in wetter locations.
